public int uniqueMorseRepresentations(String[] words) {
    String[] morseCodeMap = {".-","-...","-.-.","-..",".","..-.","--.",
                            "....","..",".---","-.-",".-..","--","-.",
                            "---",".--.","--.-",".-.","...","-","..-",
                            "...-",".--","-..-","-.--","--.."};
    Set<String> morseRepresentations = new HashSet<>();
    for (String word : words) {
        StringBuilder morseRepresentation = new StringBuilder();
        for (char c : word.toCharArray()) {
            morseRepresentation.append(morseCodeMap[c - 'a']);
        }
        morseRepresentations.add(morseRepresentation.toString());
    }
    return morseRepresentations.size();
}
```
Please note that the `String[] morseCodeMap` maps the lowercase letters of the alphabet to their corresponding Morse code representations. In this solution, we iterate through each word in the input array and build its Morse code representation by concatenating the Morse code representation for each letter. public int minInsertions(String s) {
    int leftCount = 0;
    int rightCount = 0;
    char[] chars = s.toCharArray();
    for (char c : chars) {
        if (c == '(') {
            leftCount++;
        } else if (c == ')') {
            rightCount++;
        }
    }
    return Math.abs(leftCount - rightCount);
}

public static int singleNumber(int[] nums) {
    int result = 0;
    for (int num : nums) {
        result ^= num;
    }
    return result;
}
```

### Explanation:

The solution uses the bitwise XOR operator `^` to find the element that appears only once. The XOR operator returns a value that is true if and only if the bits of the operands are different.

The first time a number `num` is encountered in the array, its XOR operation with `result` gives the same value as `num`.
```
result ^ num == num
```
The next time the same number is encountered, the XOR operation gives 0, because the bits are the same:
```
result ^ num == 0
```
What the solution does is that it keeps XORing the `nums` elements with the previous result, so if it is the first time a number is encountered, it will be equal to the number. If it is encountered again, the XOR will give 0.

Therefore, by XORing all the elements of the array together, the result will be the number that appears only once.

For the example `new int[]{2,2,3,2}`, the array would be XORed as follows:
```
2 ^ 2 = 0
0 ^ 3 = 3
3 ^ 0 = 3
```
So the final result is 3, which is the number that appears only once in the array.

This solution has a time complexity of O(n) and a space complexity of O(1), where n is the length of the array.
